newsitem.title: USA: Hope and controversy for Christopher in Africa.
newsitem.headline: Hope and controversy for Christopher in Africa.

text.p: On a recent morning in South Africa, U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher spent a half hour with nearly 200 homeless black women who are struggling with great dignity to build better lives.

On a dusty lot outside Cape Town, the women -- some with babies strapped to their backs -- deftly wielded trowels as they evenly spread mortar, transforming home-made cinder blocks into two- and three-bedroom houses costing $3,000 or less.

The homeownership programme is backed by the state and the small savings of the women members who earn susbsistence wages. The aim is to construct 150 homes at this one site. The countrywide need is one million units by the year 2000.

Christopher used the event to focus on positive trends in the new post-apartheid South Africa -- and the tangible results even small amounts of dwindling U.S. foreign aid (for technical assistance) can help produce half a world away.

The stop was one of many on his first visit to sub-Saharan Africa, a five-nation tour intended to signal a more intensive U.S. involvement in Africa. It set a high standard for U.S. President Bill Clinton if he is re-elected on Nov. 5.
But the trip also underscored the mixed U.S. record in Africa and the mixed views about what the U.S. role on that desperately poor, yet promising, continent should be.

As Christopher hop-scotched across Mali, Ethiopia, Tanzania, South Africa and Angola, he heard his country faulted for disengaging from Africa's huge black-majority underbelly. He also drew fire for trying to take the initiative away from regional leaders on several issues.
His first venture into sub-Saharan Africa also sparked a stunning dispute with France, the oldest U.S. ally, over charges of interfering in Paris' former colonial sphere of influence.
And there were complaints he flew thousands of miles for photo opportunities in a blatant appeal for Afro-American votes three weeks before the U.S. presidential election.

Critics have a point when they complain sub-Saharan Africa has not had the kind of sustained U.S. attention deserved by a region of 700 million people, where there are some encourging signs of movement toward economic and political reform.

Clinton in 1993 declared Africa a priority. He has never been there and rarely talks about the subject, although other senior aides, like National Security Adviser Anthony Lake, an Africa expert, have visited the continent.
Also, while Christopher has long wanted to visit the region, he only fit the trip in at the end of his term -- some say close to the election in a bid to lure U.S. black voters.
The administration has reason to avoid Africa, which many equate only with starvation, poverty and hopelessness.

U.S. involvement in Somalia in 1992-93, which shifted from preventing famine to nation-building, led to the death of 18 American servicemen on Clinton's watch and made Washington disinclined to intervene directly in African crises.
Liberia, founded by freed American slaves, came closest to being a U.S. colonial interest but Washington has largely washed its hands of the civil war and ensuing chaos there.
Still, Christopher insisted on his trip that the United States has an interest in Africa and "would not walk away."
He had several goals, including persuading African leaders to provide troops for an all-African military force that Washington would bankroll for intervening in crises as needed.

Mali and Ethiopia agreed to join. But influential South Africa insisted such decisions be referred to regional groups, raising doubts about whether it could be assembled in time to be effective if Burundi, the first concern, erupts in genocide.

Christopher failed to get African leaders to propose a replacement for Egyptian Boutros Boutros-Ghali as U.N. secretary general. Officials said they believe the leaders now know Washington is serious about forcing Boutros-Ghali's ouster and will offer alternate names after the U.S. election.
Many leaders welcomed his tour and a U.S. role in Africa. But Christopher's suggestions for easing sanctions on Burundi and considering new sanctions on Nigeria did not yield results.
Whatever the controversy surrounding the trip, Christopher raised expectations for U.S. policy toward Africa over the next four years -- if Clinton is re-eleced as seems likely.
That includes more U.S. engagement, Afro-American efforts against global crime, narcotics and terrorism and a commitment to provide primary education for all African children by 2010.
